name: Medical tourism (Turkey/Istanbul/Korea)

card.summary: Travelling abroad, often to Turkey or South Korea, for cosmetic surgery, hair transplants or dental work at lower prices; reviews flag infection and follow-up-care risks.
card.aka: Turkey trip, cosmetic tourism, health tourism
card.note: Published literature on medical tourism documents infectious complications, limited aftercare and insurance gaps; outcomes vary widely by clinic.

quick.overview:
Medical tourism means travelling to another country to obtain non-emergency medical care. In appearance culture the term usually refers to surgery, hair transplants and dental work in places such as Istanbul, Antalya or South Korea, where prices can be lower than in the patient's home country.

There are no controlled trials of 'looksmaxxing trips' as such. Public-health reviews of medical tourism in general describe benefits such as access and cost, alongside complications and continuity-of-care problems.
quick.mechanism: Patients usually book through clinics or agents, travel for a package that can include surgery, accommodation and transfers, and return home within days to weeks. Follow-up care after return is arranged with local clinicians, if at all.
quick.risks: Reviews report infections (including outbreaks of fungal meningitis linked to cosmetic surgery in Mexico), difficulty arranging follow-up, and possible clotting risks with long flights after surgery. Legal recourse and insurance coverage for complications can be limited. Regulation differs by country; Turkey introduced a regulation on international health tourism in 2017.

lead: Medical tourism is travel abroad to obtain medical treatment. It once described patients moving from poorer countries to wealthy ones for specialist care; it now more often describes patients from high-income countries travelling to lower-cost destinations for surgery, dental work or fertility treatment, with cosmetic procedures a large category. [1][2]

In appearance culture the phrase usually refers to a short list of destinations and procedures. Turkey, especially Istanbul and Antalya, is known for hair transplants and for dental veneers, crowns and implants; South Korea is known for facial cosmetic surgery such as eyelid surgery, rhinoplasty and facial contouring. [1][16] People use these trips to change a specific feature (a hairline, a nose, a jaw, a smile) at a lower price than at home, to combine several procedures in one stay, or to reach surgeons with a large volume of a particular operation. [1][17][19]

Looksmaxxing forums discuss the route often: members ask for surgeon recommendations for nose and chin work in Turkey, compare Turkish and Thai surgeons, and post trip plans that bundle genioplasty, lip lift, veneers, cheek implants, brow lift, laser resurfacing and fat grafting into one stay. [18][19][21]

Academic reviews describe medical tourism as growing, and they flag infectious complications, continuity of care and legal recourse as recurring concerns. [4][5] Evidence consists mainly of reviews, case series, scoping studies and registered observational trials rather than controlled studies of appearance trips specifically.

chain: Travel to a lower-cost or high-volume destination
Hair transplant, rhinoplasty, jaw or dental work done in one package stay
Changed hairline, nose, facial structure or smile at a lower price than at home
angle.text: The procedures themselves (hair restoration, rhinoplasty, facial contouring, veneers) change appearance directly; travel mainly changes cost, scheduling and which surgeons are accessible. Many people book a package that includes the operation, accommodation and transfers, then have follow-up care at home.

paras: Scholars distinguish several forms of cross-border patient mobility. A typology paper sets out the categories, and some authors prefer the broader phrase 'movement for healthcare'. [6][7] A scoping review of patient experience found that little was known about the scope of the phenomenon, and a separate scoping review examined its effects on destination and departure countries. [8][9]

The main drivers named in reference works are high domestic prices, long waiting lists for some procedures, cheaper international travel and improved standards abroad. UK patients are described as motivated mainly by waiting times, while US patients are described as motivated mainly by price. [1] A 2008 Deloitte report cited by Wikipedia put savings in Costa Rica at 30 to 70 percent against US prices and estimated that about 750,000 Americans travelled abroad for care in 2007. [1]

Typical cosmetic packages bundle the procedure, hospital or clinic fees, hotel and airport transfers, sometimes with a coordinator or interpreter. Patients usually arrange follow-up with local clinicians after returning home. [1][5]

Wikipedia traces the earliest recorded medical travel to Greek pilgrims visiting the sanctuary of the healing god Asklepios at Epidauria, and describes 18th-century European spas drawing patients for mineral waters. [1] The modern pattern of patients from rich countries seeking cheaper elective care grew in the 2000s as flights became cheaper and hospitals in Asia, Latin America and Turkey marketed to foreign patients. [1][2][10]

A 2010 review in Maturitas assessed the evidence on treatment abroad and found it largely descriptive. [2] Two 2010 scoping reviews, on patient experience and on effects on destination and departure countries, mapped how little systematic data existed. [8][9] In 2004 the WHO launched the World Alliance for Patient Safety, which Wikipedia lists among oversight efforts relevant to cross-border care. [1]

Turkey is described as an affordable hub for hair transplant surgery, and dental treatments such as veneers, crowns and implants are offered in Istanbul, Ankara and Antalya. [1] Wikipedia's hair transplantation article gives an average price per graft of US$1.07 in Turkey against US$7.00 in Canada. [17] Roughly 178,000 health tourists visited in the first half of 2018, about two-thirds of them treated in private hospitals. [1]

Turkey's Regulation on International Health Tourism and Tourist Health took effect on 13 July 2017 and applies to people who travel specifically for treatment. In 2019 the Ministry of Health established USHAS to promote and regulate the sector. [1]

Hair transplants are performed mostly with follicular unit extraction (FUE), in which individual one-to-four-hair units are removed from the back of the scalp with 0.6 to 1.0 mm punches under local anesthesia and implanted in thinning areas. Recovery is described as under a week, and the technique leaves small punctate scars. [17] Wikipedia notes that FUE has a demanding surgeon learning curve and that some surgeons report a lower ratio of successful grafts than with strip harvesting. [17] Temporary thinning ('shock loss') is described as common after any hair transplant. [17]
On looksmax.org, members compare Turkish surgeons for rhinoplasty and chin work, discuss hair transplants that went poorly, and post accounts of multi-procedure stays in Antalya. [18][20][24]

As of 2021, ISAPS data placed South Korea first in the world for elective cosmetic surgery per capita, and Wikipedia reports that about one in five Korean women has had a procedure. [16] The country's cosmetic-surgery culture is linked in that account to the physiognomy tradition of gwansang, to the introduction of plastic surgery techniques by American doctors during the Korean War, to job-market competition after the 1997 Asian financial crisis, and to K-pop and K-drama. [16]

In 2018, 464,452 medical tourists visited Korea for cosmetic surgery, up 16.7 percent from 2017. [16] Commonly performed operations include double-eyelid surgery, rhinoplasty (the most common surgery among ethnic Koreans) and facial contouring, often called V-line surgery, which reduces the cheekbones or jaw. [16] A surgeon cited in the article describes facial contouring as complex, with long swelling and risks including permanent numbness. [16]

The same article describes the 'ghost surgery' controversy, in which a substitute surgeon operates while the patient is anesthetised. The Korean Society of Plastic Surgeons estimated about 100,000 victims from 2008 to 2014, and public backlash led to a mandate for cameras in operating rooms. [16]

Wikipedia lists Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Czech Republic, the Dominican Republic, Egypt, Greece, Iran, India, Italy, Lebanon, Malaysia, Mexico, Poland, Thailand, Turkey and South Korea among cosmetic-surgery destinations. [1] Dental tourism clusters include Los Algodones in Mexico and Mosonmagyarovar in Hungary. [1] Looksmaxxing forum threads comparing surgeons name Thailand alongside Turkey. [21]

No studies found of travel for appearance procedures to Turkey or South Korea as a defined intervention. Related research covers medical tourism generally: reviews of infectious complications, scoping reviews of patient experience, and registered trials that look at venous changes during long-haul flights after aesthetic surgery. [4][8][10][11]

The registered flight studies are observational or randomized designs measuring popliteal vein diameter after air travel following aesthetic surgery, comparing for example cabin class and graduated compression stockings. [10][11][22][23] A further registered study looks at anxiety among bariatric health tourists. [15]

A 2024 review of the previous 18 months found an increase in reported infectious complications in patients who had received care abroad, often with prolonged morbidity, repeat treatment and hospital stays, and occasionally deaths. It described an outbreak of fungal meningitis among US residents who had epidural anesthesia for cosmetic surgery in two Mexican clinics: 31 cases with severe cerebrovascular complications and eight deaths as of July 2023. [4]

A 2019 JAMA article reviewed infections linked to medical tourism. Other papers discuss carriage of multi-resistant bacteria between health systems and the spread of resistant organisms in destinations that are major medical-tourism hubs. [12][13][14]

Wikipedia reports that the CDC has recorded adverse events among US patients of cosmetic surgery in the Dominican Republic since 2003, and that 93 US citizens died after cosmetic surgery there from 2009 to 2022, 90 percent of autopsy-confirmed deaths being due to embolism. [1]

General sources also list unfamiliar local infections, variable post-operative care, limited follow-up after return, clot risk from flying soon after surgery, sun exposure darkening scars, and difficulty obtaining insurance or legal remedies. Patients refused treatment at home for risk reasons may also struggle to get cover for complications. [1][5]
For hair transplants, sources describe temporary shock loss, bald patches, and reduced graft survival with smoking or alcohol. [17]

Forum members present medical travel as a way to afford several procedures, ask for surgeon recommendations by procedure, and post planned itineraries and updates. [18][19][21][24] The same communities also discuss disappointing outcomes, such as a thread on a hair transplant in Turkey that went wrong. [20]

Related practices discussed alongside this route include rhinoplasty, genioplasty, cheek implants, veneers and hair restoration; the destination is treated as a variable separate from the surgeon. [18][19]

Registered studies include observational and randomized work on popliteal vein diameter during long-haul flights after aesthetic surgery and a study of anxiety in bariatric health tourism. [10][11][15][22][23] A 2024 ISAPS analysis of global aesthetic statistics, covering 34.9 million procedures by plastic surgeons in 2023, included questions on medical tourism prevalence. [3]

timeline.event: Croatia's Hygienic Association of Hvar is founded, cited as a candidate for Europe's oldest health-tourism destination. [1]
The Asian financial crisis intensifies job-market competition in South Korea, cited as a factor in cosmetic surgery demand. [16]
WHO launches the World Alliance for Patient Safety. [1]
About 750,000 Americans travel abroad for care, per a Deloitte estimate cited on Wikipedia. [1]
NeoGraft becomes the first robotic hair-restoration device cleared by the FDA. [17]
Scoping reviews map patient experience and country effects of medical tourism. [8][9]
Turkey's Regulation on International Health Tourism takes effect (13 July). [1]
464,452 medical tourists visit South Korea for cosmetic surgery; almost 178,000 health tourists visit Turkey in the first half of the year. [16][1]
Turkey's Ministry of Health establishes USHAS; JAMA reviews medical tourism-linked infections. [1][12]
Fungal meningitis outbreak reported among US patients who had cosmetic surgery with epidural anesthesia in Mexican clinics. [4]
ISAPS reports 34.9 million aesthetic procedures by plastic surgeons for 2023. [3]

lore.intro: Looksmaxxing forums discuss Turkey and Korea as routes to cheaper or more specialised procedures, with threads asking for surgeon recommendations and others reporting outcomes. [18][19][20]

claims.claim: Turkey is the cost-effective place to get hair or face surgery
claims.believers: Members ask for Turkish surgeons for nose and chin work and post trips combining many procedures in Antalya, citing price and surgeon volume. [18][19][24]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists average hair graft prices of US$1.07 in Turkey against US$7.00 in Canada, and reviews say cost is a main driver of medical tourism. [1][17]

claims.claim: Several procedures can be stacked into one trip
claims.believers: A looksmax.org member posted a plan for genioplasty, lip lift, veneers, cheek implants, brow lift, laser resurfacing and fat grafts in one stay. [19]
claims.experts: Reviews note that long flights soon after surgery raise clot risk, and registered trials are measuring vein changes after post-surgical flights. [1][10][22]

claims.claim: Choosing the surgeon matters more than the country
claims.believers: Threads compare named surgeons in Turkey and Thailand and ask for recommendations by procedure. [18][21]
claims.experts: Reviews describe variable quality between hospitals and countries and limited follow-up after return, and Wikipedia describes Korean 'ghost surgery' where a substitute operates. [1][5][16]

claims.claim: Korea is the destination for facial contouring
claims.believers: Korea is discussed for jaw and cheek reduction and eyelid work, reflecting its high procedure volume. [16]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports Korea has the highest per-capita cosmetic surgery rate and describes facial contouring as complex, with long swelling and risks including numbness. [16]

claims.claim: Hair transplants in Turkey can go wrong, so results vary by clinic
claims.believers: Forum members post accounts of poor outcomes after Turkish hair transplants. [20]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes shock loss and variable graft survival, and a 2024 review reports rising infectious complications after care abroad. [4][17]

claims.believers: Travellers plan to follow up with local clinicians after returning. [19]
claims.experts: Reviews describe limited aftercare, difficulty obtaining insurance cover and unfamiliar legal systems for complications. [1][4][5]
